faq.question: Does offering food establish self-preservation Type Two?

faq.answer: Record direct requests, offers, refusals, resource limits, and later statements. Treat an indirect expectation as a hypothesis only when the person confirms it or repeated behavior provides specific evidence.
faq.question: How can receiving care be observed without mind-reading?

faq.answer: Directly stated needs, support that changes mainly with budget, or stronger recurring attention to group roles or one intense bond would weaken it. Household and access conditions should be examined first.

sections.body_md: The hypothesis combines Type Two needs-and-connection attention with a self-preservation label for comfort, support, and resource exchange. Practical warmth may instead reflect household custom, scarcity, disability access, hospitality, caregiving, or a direct agreement.
sections.title: Frame practical connection provisionally

sections.body_md: This matched comparison asks about practical comfort and group role by observing whether attention first moves toward receiving care, a useful place in the group, or concentrated connection with one person. Keep the request, resources, and relationship stakes as similar as possible.
sections.title: Compare three priorities in one exchange

sections.body_md: Self-preservation is traditional organizing vocabulary. It is not evidence about bodily mechanisms. It makes no claims about neural organization or fixed functions, and it cannot establish health, universal priorities, or automatic needs shared by every person.
sections.title: Keep self-preservation descriptive

sections.body_md: Subtype traditions differ about whether self-preservation Two looks more openly needy, playful, guarded, or countertypical. Test one observable proposition at a time and let direct communication or environmental facts replace the portrait.
sections.title: Allow indirect and countertypical descriptions to vary

sections.body_md: Tight budgets, food traditions, chronic workload, disability access, caring for dependents, or recent instability can organize practical support. Compare safer periods and other households before assigning a subtype explanation.
sections.title: Test scarcity, access, and household norms

sections.body_md: A self-preservation Type Two counterexample weakens an indirect receiving-care hypothesis when needs are stated directly, practical exchange changes with resources, or matched situations consistently prioritize group contribution or one focused bond.
sections.title: Use direct requests as disconfirming evidence

sections.body_md: Subtype findings are instrument-specific and do not justify broad cultural or individual conclusions. Retain mixed cases, explicit consent, direct requests, and environmental alternatives.
sections.title: Keep subtype conclusions narrow

sections.body_md:
Duration: 5

Context: Choose one meal or comfort exchange, one resource-limited request, and one moment when the person needs support themselves.

Observable signal: Record what was offered, what was requested directly, which resource limit was named, and how care was accepted, declined, or sought later.

Page-specific signal: Compare practical comfort and indirect receiving with group contribution and focused one-person connection in similar requests.

Alternative explanation: Test household culture, scarcity, disability access, caregiving, hospitality, workload, and recent instability against the subtype.

Reflection prompt: Identify the clearest direct request and explain whether it weakens an indirect receiving-care interpretation or only refines it.

seo.description: Self-preservation Type Two is a traditional type-by-instinct hypothesis in which Two attention to connection may appear through comfort, practical support, resource exchange, and indirect ways of receiving care. Two receiving care is an observation target, not evidence about bodily mechanisms or a universal subtype.
seo.title: Self-preservation Type Two: receiving care as a traditional hypothesis
